title: Transactional Tribunal Infrastructure :Toward a Harmonized Real-Time Transactional Trust Infrastructure – « A Framework for Global Transaction Certification, Dynamic Arbitration, and Programmable Procedural Fairness »

detail.title: Transactional Tribunal Infrastructure :Toward a Harmonized Real-Time Transactional Trust Infrastructure – « A Framework for Global Transaction Certification, Dynamic Arbitration, and Programmable Procedural Fairness »
detail.abstract: Global digital commerce suffers from fragmented payment systems, opaque logistics, unenforceable SLAs, and asymmetric access to trust. This paper proposes the Harmonized Transactional Tribunal—a voluntary, real‑time, programmable trust infrastructure for cross‑border transactions. Drawing on transaction cost economics, game theory, procedural justice, and cryptographic verification, we specify a five‑layer architecture: (1) transactional identity and cryptographic sealing using DIDs and verifiable credentials; (2) real‑time monitoring and event sourcing; (3) behavioral scoring and SLA enforcement using beta reputation models; (4) hybrid AI/human arbitration with automated conditional compensation and human‑in‑the‑loop appeals; and (5) dynamic, portable certification. The tribunal adopts existing standards (ISO 20022, SWIFT gpi, W3C VCs) and open APIs to enable third‑party innovation. We analyze use cases in cross‑border e‑commerce, B2B supply chain finance, freelancing, trade finance, and insurance. Risks—algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, regulatory conflict, exclusion—are mitigated through transparency, independent audits, multi‑stakeholder governance, and adaptive standards. We conclude that programmable procedural fairness is feasible with existing technology; the missing component is collective action to build shared infrastructure. The tribunal offers a path from fragmented, opaque, asymmetric trust to harmonized, transparent, verifiable trust for all participants.

title: A Comparative Study between Hybrid ML Models and Few-Shot In-Context LLM Models for Detecting Non-Actionable Email in a Customer-Service Setting
affiliations: National Institute of Development Administration and National Institute of Development Administration

detail.title: A Comparative Study between Hybrid ML Models and Few-Shot In-Context LLM Models for Detecting Non-Actionable Email in a Customer-Service Setting
detail.abstract: In customer service, non-actionable emails—such as auto-replies, acknowledgments, and system notifications are also considered spam because they disrupt agent workflow, overwhelm queues, and reduce operational efficiency despite not being harmful. We investigate detection of these non-actionable emails in the customer-service domain, where not all incoming messages require agent intervention. Unlike traditional email spam classifiers focused on malicious or promotional content, our objective is to identify non-actionable messages that do not require attention. To address this challenge, we compare two methodological approaches: (1) a hybrid ML model, a traditional machine learning (ML) classifier enhanced with a confidence-aware, rule-augmented hybrid ML pipeline that integrates calibration-derived uncertainty zones with domain-informed override rules, and (2) a few-shot LLM-based model using prompt engineering tailored to domain-specific semantics. On our in-house dataset, experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid ML model, notably SVM, achieved a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 84% and 98% precision, while the GPT-4o-mini achieved 83% MCC and 98% precision better than the other free and paid LLM models. These findings highlight the effectiveness of both approaches in improving semantic-aware email classification, especially the hybrid approach detects non-actionable emails as accurately as the LLM approach while favoring lower cost, greater controllability, and seamless integration into existing email-processing systems. This work offers a practical and interpretable framework for operational use and lays the groundwork for future systems capable of adapting to evolving communication patterns in customer service settings.

title: A Parallel Physics-Data Fusion Network with Auto-Adaptive Gating for Thermal Runaway Prediction in Lithium-Ion Batteries
affiliations: Hefei University of Technology - School of Automotive and Transportation Engineering, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology - School of Automotive and Transportation Engineering and Hefei University of Technology

detail.title: A Parallel Physics-Data Fusion Network with Auto-Adaptive Gating for Thermal Runaway Prediction in Lithium-Ion Batteries
detail.abstract: Purely data-driven models for lithium-ion battery thermal runaway prediction often suffer from poor cross-condition generalization, whereas physics-based approaches struggle to capture complex temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose a Parallel Physics-Data Fusion Network (PPDF-Net), which integrates a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network within a dual-branch parallel architecture, combined with an adaptive gated fusion mechanism. The model simultaneously predicts the temperature field and reactant concentration. Training data were generated from a coupled model combining two-dimensional axisymmetric thermo-physical fields with global reaction kinetics under multiple ambient temperatures. Results demonstrate that PPDF-Net achieves high accuracy on in-distribution data, with a temperature Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.58 K (R2 = 0.9997) and a concentration R2 of 0.9996. Under unseen conditions, the model maintains strong generalization (temperature R2 > 0.88, concentration R2 > 0.98) and robustness, with a temperature MAE below 7 K under 15% input noise. Compared with Deep Neural Network (DNN), Pure LSTM, and Pure PINN baselines, PPDF-Net demonstrates superior generalization and noise tolerance. These findings highlight the effectiveness of physics-data fusion with adaptive gating, indicating strong potential for deployment in real-world battery management systems.

title: End-to-end Framework for Autonomous Building Control Deployment via Domain-Randomized Reinforcement Learning and Arbitration Policy Selection
affiliations: Purdue University, Purdue University and Purdue University

detail.title: End-to-end Framework for Autonomous Building Control Deployment via Domain-Randomized Reinforcement Learning and Arbitration Policy Selection
detail.abstract: ​The paper presents an end-to-end framework for autonomous building control that integrates domain-randomized reinforcement learning (DR-RL) with Arbitration Policy Selection (APS) to handle variability across policy development, adaptation, and long-term operation under real deployment conditions. During development, domain randomization generates a diverse set of plausible building environments from limited prior information, enabling pretraining that exposes policies to variability in building models without requiring source–target similarity assumptions. During initial field deployment, APS automatically selects the most suitable pretrained policy based on short-term operational performance, mitigating negative transfer and eliminating the need for retraining or accurate target models. During long-term operation, the learning-based control policies continue to adapt to previously unseen conditions, enabling sustained performance under evolving real-world dynamics without requiring manual intervention.The proposed approach is first validated using simulations for a single-zone and multi-zone DOE reference building, where APS-selected policies achieve 11.5%–50.6% improvements in initial performance and 37.4%–50.0% gains in long-term performance, compared to training from scratch, while reducing adaptation time from multiple weeks to less than two days. The framework is further evaluated in an actual office building, achieving 7.8%–10% reward improvement and 13.6%–15.9% energy reduction over baseline control while maintaining thermal comfort. Following a short adaptation phase, the approach rapidly stabilizes and consistently outperforms baseline rule-based control and RL policy trained on nominal building model) under real-world deployment conditions. Beyond performance improvement, the developed framework reduces setup to a minimal configuration process requiring less than one day of low-dimensional input specification, after which policy generation, evaluation, and selection are performed automatically. In both simulation and field deployment, the results show that combining DR-RL with APS provides a practical pathway toward scalable deployment of advanced control systems and offers a foundation for AI-driven building operation with minimal human intervention.

title: Hard-constrained Physics-informed Neural Networks for Interface Problems
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Sandia National Laboratories, Government of the United States of America - Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

detail.title: Hard-constrained Physics-informed Neural Networks for Interface Problems
detail.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a flexible framework for solving partial differential equations, but their performance on interface problems remains challenging because continuity and flux conditions are typically imposed through soft penalty terms. The standard soft-constraint formulation leads to imperfect interface enforcement and degraded accuracy near interfaces. We introduce two ansatz-based hard-constrained PINN formulations for interface problems that embed the interface physics into the solution representation and thereby decouple interface enforcement from PDE residual minimization. The first, termed the windowing approach, constructs the trial space from compactly supported windowed subnetworks so that interface continuity and flux balance are satisfied by design. The second, called the buffer approach, augments unrestricted subnetworks with auxiliary buffer functions that enforce boundary and interface constraints at discrete points through a lightweight correction. We study these formulations on one- and two-dimensional elliptic interface benchmarks and compare them with soft-constrained baselines. In one-dimensional problems, hard constraints consistently improve interface fidelity and remove the need for loss-weight tuning; the windowing approach attains very high accuracy (as low as O(10−9)) on simple structured cases, whereas the buffer approach remains accurate (∼ O(10−5)) across a wider range of source terms and interface configurations. In two dimensions, the buffer formulation is shown to be more robust because it enforces constraints through a discrete buffer correction, as the windowing construction becomes more sensitive to overlap and corner effects and over-constrains the problem. This positions the buffer method as a straightforward and geometrically flexible approach that can be applied to complex interface problems.

title: Evaluative Favorability and Student Judgments of AI-Assisted Assessment in Business Education: Fairness, Actionability, and Baseline AI Acceptance
affiliations: University of Georgia

detail.title: Evaluative Favorability and Student Judgments of AI-Assisted Assessment in Business Education: Fairness, Actionability, and Baseline AI Acceptance
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being considered not only as a learning tool but also as a support mechanism for assessment in business education. This shift is consequential because many business-school assignments, including case analyses, strategy reports, and managerial recommendations, require interpretive judgment rather than simple answer matching. This study examines students’ episode-level perceptions of two simulated AI-assisted grading artifacts that shared a common assignment context and rubric structure but differed in evaluative favorability. Using a within-subjects design with undergraduate business students enrolled in marketing courses (N = 191), participants evaluated a higher-score, more favorable artifact and a lower-score, more critical artifact presented in randomized order. Results showed that the higher-score artifact was rated as fairer than the lower-score artifact, although the effect was modest. In contrast, perceived actionability/usefulness did not differ reliably across artifacts. Baseline AI acceptance moderated fairness judgments: students with lower initial acceptance of AI-assisted grading showed stronger favorability-based fairness differences, whereas students with higher acceptance were less reactive to the artifact contrast. The findings suggest that, in simulated AI-assisted assessment episodes, students may distinguish between feedback usefulness and fairness of evaluative judgment. The findings should not be interpreted as evidence about reactions to personally consequential course grades.

title: Forecasting Sectoral Electricity Consumption in the Selected European Countries: Machine Learning versus Deep Learning Models
affiliations: and AGH University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Forecasting Sectoral Electricity Consumption in the Selected European Countries: Machine Learning versus Deep Learning Models

keywords.keywords: Sectoral electricity forecastingDeep LearningMachine LearningElectrificationGrid planningEuropean Energy Systems

detail.abstract: Sector-level electricity demand forecasting remains underexplored in multi-country energy systems despite its importance for grid planning, electrification, and decarbonization. This study develops a comparative forecasting framework for 266 annual sector-country time series covering 14 sectors in 19 European countries from 1995 to 2023. It contributes to benchmarking statistical, machine learning, and deep learning models under a unified empirical setting and assesses model robustness across heterogeneous sectors and national energy systems. Five approaches—ARIMA, SVM, Random Forest, LSTM, and CNN–BiLSTM–AR— were evaluated. Forecasting performance varies markedly across sectors and countries; Random Forest achieves the lowest forecasting errors in most sector-country cases and the best overall accuracy (MAPE = 8.31%), followed by ARIMA (MAPE = 9.84%), while LSTM and SVM show weaker average performances. Diebold–Mariano tests indicate that Random Forest, LSTM, and SVM outperform ARIMA in most comparisons. The results show that ensemble-based nonlinear methods, especially random forests, provide a robust approach to long-term sectoral electricity demand forecasting in Europe, with implications for grid planning, electrification, and energy system optimization.

title: Assessing Hydrogen Deployment Potential in Nigeria: A Site-Based Assessment of Industrial Infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Manchester Metropolitan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Assessing Hydrogen Deployment Potential in Nigeria: A Site-Based Assessment of Industrial Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Hydrogen is increasingly recognized as a key pathway for decarbonizing energy systems and supporting the global transition toward low-carbon energy. However, limited studies systematically examine how existing industrial infrastructure can enable hydrogen deployment in emerging energy economies. In countries such as Nigeria, understanding the spatial distribution of energy infrastructure is essential for identifying feasible hydrogen deployment pathways. This study presents a site-based assessment framework for hydrogen deployment potential across sixty-two (62) facilities within the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) asset portfolio, classified into production, storage and distribution, asset management, and administrative categories. A multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) framework is applied to evaluate and rank sites based on infrastructure readiness and enabling conditions. The results indicate that refinery and depot clusters in Port Harcourt, Warri, Kaduna, Calabar, and Benin offer strong near-term opportunities for blue hydrogen development, while northern regions exhibit longer-term potential for solar-based green hydrogen production. Geologically stable areas in Benue, Cross River, and Enugu also present promising prospects for natural hydrogen exploration. Gas metering stations emerge as important integration nodes within a future hydrogen value chain, supported by administrative and operational hubs. A phased development pathway links early pilot projects with medium-term logistics hubs and long-term hydrogen valley development, providing a data-driven foundation for strategic hydrogen deployment in Nigeria and offering insights relevant to hydrogen planning in other emerging energy systems.

title: Markovian Financial Contagion in Heterogeneous Interbank Networks:Stochastic Panic, Capital Stratification, and the Circuit Breaker as a Macroprudential Tool
affiliations: Instituto Politécnico Nacional

detail.title: Markovian Financial Contagion in Heterogeneous Interbank Networks:Stochastic Panic, Capital Stratification, and the Circuit Breaker as a Macroprudential Tool
detail.abstract: We present a Markovian agent-based model of financial contagion in directed interbank networks, extending the canonical binary-state (solvent/defaulted) framework to a three-state system that explicitly models financial distress as an intermediate, recoverable condition. The model introduces five novel contributions relative to prior work: (i) a three-state Markov chain {Solvent, Distressed, Defaulted} governing individual bank dynamics; (ii) endogenous stochastic panic proportional to the real-time systemic default rate ; (iii) discrete capital heterogeneity creating two structurally distinct bank classes (small and large); (iv) a market circuit breaker policy that suspends contagion transmission once defaults exceed a regulatory threshold; and (v) a cross-bank distress correlation heatmap as an econometric tool for identifying systemic clusters. The model is calibrated to the Mexican banca múltiple ( institutions, network density , ICAP distribution at December 2025) using CNBV and Banxico supervisory data, providing the first quantitative assessment of circuit-breaker design for a Latin American financial system. Using banks, connectivity , and Monte Carlo replications, we characterise the interaction of these mechanisms and derive policy implications for macroprudential regulation. We show that the circuit breaker is effective in the transitional connectivity regime but insufficient against fully supercritical cascades; that the calibrated Mexican system operates at the subcritical–transitional boundary where circuit-breaker activation would reduce systemic defaults by up to 39.6%; and that the correlation heatmap reveals structured cluster formation that is invisible to aggregate metrics alone.

title: Silent Corruption: Logic Collapse and Attribution Fidelity Failure in Compressed Intrusion Detection Systems
affiliations: , Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications and Incheon National University

detail.title: Silent Corruption: Logic Collapse and Attribution Fidelity Failure in Compressed Intrusion Detection Systems
detail.abstract: Model compression is essential for deploying intrusion detection systems (IDS) on edge and IoT hardware, yet compressed models are evaluated solely on classification accuracy. This leaves a critical question unanswered: does compression preserve not only what a model predicts, but why? We show that it does not. We term this failure Silent Corruption: a compressed IDS model maintains high accuracy while its SHAP attribution logic is silently corrupted, with no accuracy-based monitor raising any warning. The underlying mechanism, Logic Collapse, causes attribution vectors to shift toward entirely different features than the original model, misleading analysts into investigating the wrong causes. Across four IDS benchmarks and two architectures, 4-bit quantization triggers Logic Collapse in seven of eight configurations and knowledge distillation in all eight, despite all configurations retaining over 98.9% accuracy. Logic Collapse is further shown to be actively exploitable within normal operational accuracy variance. To address it, we propose LoRA-SHAP, the first LoRA-based compression method for tabular IDS classifiers that embeds SHAP attribution fidelity as a training objective, paired with SPLRA for sensitivity-guided rank allocation. LoRA-SHAP achieves a 96.9% safe explanation rate, a 74-point gain over vanilla LoRA (Wilcoxon p<0.01), with under 0.2% accuracy loss and no added inference cost.

title: Deep learning-based bias correction and multi-index drought assessment across Europe using CMIP6 projections
affiliations: University of Galway, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Galway and University of Galway

detail.title: Deep learning-based bias correction and multi-index drought assessment across Europe using CMIP6 projections
detail.abstract: Drought is a complex, multi-stage phenomenon that propagates through the hydrological cycle, linking atmospheric forcing with soil moisture and runoff responses. Reliable assessment of future drought risk under climate change requires hydro-climatic variables with reduced systematic biases. This study develops an integrated drought assessment framework across Europe by combining deep learning-based bias correction with a multi-index analysis using the Standardized Precipitation Index(SPI), Standardized Soil Moisture Index(SSI), and Standardized Runoff Index(SRI). CMIP6 precipitation, soil moisture, and surface runoff are bias-corrected using a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory(ConvLSTM ) model, with ERA5-Land as the reference dataset. Unlike conventional approaches that treat variables independently, the proposed framework applies spatio-temporal bias correction consistently across multiple hydro-climatic variables before integrating them into a unified drought assessment. The ConvLSTM model substantially improves the representation of hydro-climatic variables, with the strongest improvement observed for surface runoff. Across the corrected variables, correlations increase considerably, while root mean square error and bias are markedly reduced in both training and testing periods. These improvements show that the model captures spatio-temporal dependencies and limits the propagation of systematic climate-model errors into drought indices. The corrected SPI, SSI, and SRI results reveal a clear intensification of future drought conditions across Europe, with strong spatial and seasonal contrasts. Drought signals are most pronounced in southern and central Europe, especially during the warm season, while northern regions show weaker and more heterogeneous responses. The multi-index results also indicate a transition from rapid meteorological drought responses to delayed soil moisture and runoff responses. Overall, future droughts are projected to become more persistent, severe, and spatially extensive across Europe.​

title: A Hybrid Physics-Informed SMAP-LSTM Framework for Monthly Streamow Forecasting in a Data-Scarce Semi-Arid Basin: Application to the Utinga River Basin, Bahia, Brazil
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Hybrid Physics-Informed SMAP-LSTM Framework for Monthly Streamow Forecasting in a Data-Scarce Semi-Arid Basin: Application to the Utinga River Basin, Bahia, Brazil
detail.abstract: Accurate streamflow forecasting in semi-arid basins remains an operational challenge due to data scarcity, intermittent flow regimes, and rainfall–runoff non-linearity. We propose and evaluate a hybrid framework coupling the monthly SMAP rainfall-runoff model with Bidirectional LSTM and XGBoost, applied to the Utinga River Basin (Paraguaçu region, Bahia, Northeast Brazil; ≈1,200 km², Köppen BSh). SMAP is calibrated via Differential Evolution to extract eight physics-informed state variables (soil moisture, baseflow, recharge, surface runoff, evapotranspiration), used as input features for the data-driven models. Using 340 monthly records (1992–2021), an ablation study across five configurations shows that under severe data scarcity, standalone SMAP (NSE=0.132) outperforms purely data-driven BiLSTM variants (NSE≤−0.21). Physics-informed features improve BiLSTM test NSE by 20 percentage points; the SMAP+XGBoost hybrid achieves the best test performance (NSE=0.205). The calibrated SMAP yields Q90=0.975 m³/s, supporting the 80%×Q90 water concession limit under Bahia State legislation. The full open-source Python implementation is released on Zenodo.

title: Selective Supervision and the Incidence of Compliance Costs: Evidence from U.S. Mortgage Nonbanks, 2009–2017
affiliations: ESCP Business School

detail.title: Selective Supervision and the Incidence of Compliance Costs: Evidence from U.S. Mortgage Nonbanks, 2009–2017
detail.abstract: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s January 2012 operationalization of Section 1024 supervisory authority over U.S. mortgage nonbanks is the first natural experiment of partial federal supervision in a previously unsupervised consumer-finance segment. A differentiated-products Bertrand model of dual-channel mortgage origination yields three predictions and one negative control: positive pass-through; concentration where per-loan compliance overhead is highest and demand most inelastic; intensive-margin loading; and a null VA-only differential. A matched same-state difference-in-differences against a depository control universe purified of CFPB-supervised large depositories confirms all four. Conditional rate spreads at treated nonbanks widen by +12.5 basis points (95% CI [+3.7, +21.2]; p = 0.005) — $294 in year-one interest and $3,567 in 30-year present value on the median $235,000 origination. The widening concentrates in FHA-heavy nonbanks (+20.1 bps), is null on the VA-only split, and loads on the conditional-spread margin. A complete-prewindow placebo is quiet; leave-one-out, wild-cluster bootstrap, Romano–Wolf-adjusted heterogeneity, and a 41,233-loan supplement preserve the result. The implied aggregate transfer to FHA-heavy borrowers — disproportionately Black, Hispanic, and lower-income — is approximately $1.43 billion in 30-year present value ($0.6–$1.7 billion across the full sensitivity band), and the model characterizes directionally the welfare incidence under activity-based and size-graduated counterfactual architectures.

title: Financial Literacy, Risk Tolerance, and Household Saving Behaviour: Evidence from the UK Cost-of-Living Crisis
affiliations: Coventry University

detail.title: Financial Literacy, Risk Tolerance, and Household Saving Behaviour: Evidence from the UK Cost-of-Living Crisis
detail.abstract: Household financial fragility poses systemic risks that prudential regulators increasingly recognise as material to financial stability. Yet the micro-level mechanisms through which financial literacy either buffers or fails to buffer households against macroeconomic stress remain poorly understood. This paper addresses that gap using nationally representative data from the UK Household Financial Survey (UKHFS) 2021, collected at the onset of the sharpest UK rate cycle in four decades, during which approximately 1.6 million fixed-rate mortgage deals expired, exposing households to payment shocks averaging £500 per month. We find that financial literacy exerts a significant positive effect on household saving rates (β = 0.27, p < .001), with 42% of this effect transmitted through risk tolerance as a partial mediator. Critically, this protective mechanism is heterogeneous and fragility-amplifying in its distributional consequences. Among lower-income households the indirect effect collapses (γ = 0.09 versus γ = 0.26 for higher-income households), because structural risk aversion, rooted in thin financial buffers and high income volatility, suppresses the behavioural translation of financial knowledge. We term this the knowledge–activation gap: financial literacy reaches vulnerable households but fails to activate the risk-tolerant behaviour that converts knowledge into saving and sound mortgage management. Three contributions follow. The paper formalises the literacy–tolerance–saving pathway as a theoretically grounded partial mediation model tested through bootstrapped indirect effects and structural equation modelling. It provides the first UK evidence linking financial literacy and risk tolerance jointly to mortgage decision outcomes, product selection, overpayment, and proactive remortgaging. Finally, it demonstrates that knowledge–activation asymmetry concentrates financial fragility precisely among households most exposed to rate shocks, with direct implications for macro-prudential policy design.

title: Quantifying Ghana’s Mining Expansion: Combining MiningPolygons, Transition Rules and zone-specific Random Forestmodels
affiliations: Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Quantifying Ghana’s Mining Expansion: Combining MiningPolygons, Transition Rules and zone-specific Random Forestmodels
detail.abstract: Ghana is witnessing a rapid expansion of mining, especially in its south-western forestzone. This expansion, visible and measurable from space using remote sensing, introducesprofound changes for the people living in these areas. Accurately quantifying the timingand extent of these changes is important to evaluate policies, sustainability, and develop-ment outcomes. Whilst earlier remote sensing studies on Ghana have focused on shortertime periods, smaller areas of interest, or applied a single national classification model,not taking into account distinct ecological zones, I suggest using known mining locations,transition rules, and zone-specific models to better capture Ghana’s changing landscapes.Using Landsat time series from 2000 to 2019, developing ensemble random forest mod-els for each of Ghana’s distinct ecological zones, and applying backward transition rules,I estimate historical mining expansion within known mining boundaries. Constrainingclassification to known mining areas enables an improved assessment of mining-relatedland conversion including mine infrastructure and tailings, while backward transition rulesprevented ecologically implausible transitions between landcover classes. Results indi-cate Ghana’s mining area expanded from approximately 1,375 ha in 2000 to 42,410 ha in2019, with peak expansion occurring during 2011 to 2013, and from 2016 onwards. Myapproach demonstrates that recent improvements in remote sensing can be used to trainclassification models for better historical analyses of lower resolution and lower qualityimagery. My results, although focused on Ghana, offer relevant methodological insightsand improvements for land cover analyses globally.

title: Deep Learning-Based Test Smell Prediction Using Hybrid AST Sequence Representations
affiliations: Quy Nhon University, The University of Danang and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Deep Learning-Based Test Smell Prediction Using Hybrid AST Sequence Representations
detail.abstract: Test smells indicate poor test code quality, degrading test effectiveness and maintainability. Most prior studies on test smell prediction have predominantly relied on software metric-based approaches, which often result in limited predictive performance. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a deep learning (DL)-based approach for test smell prediction that leverages sequence-level representations of test code. Specifically, we construct a novel dataset, named SeqTS, in which test methods are encoded as hybrid Abstract Syntax Tree-based token sequences, preserving both structural information and contextual interaction patterns. Extensive experiments are conducted using four DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory, Gated Recurrent Unit, and Transformer, under within-project and cross-project scenarios for three representative test smells, namely Eager Test, Mystery Guest, and Resource Optimism. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce a sequence-level dataset derived directly from ASTs for test smell prediction, along with a systematic evaluation of multiple DL architectures across diverse experimental settings. The results demonstrate that the SeqTS dataset effectively enhances the performance of DL-based predictors. Moreover, the proposed predictors consistently outperform baseline methods across all evaluation metrics. Notably, the CNN-based predictor achieves an F1-score improvement exceeding 29\% compared to the software metric-based baseline for Eager Test. This study also conducts a comprehensive evaluation through ablation studies and statistical analyses, thereby providing deeper insights into the effectiveness and limitations of the proposed approach while highlighting key directions for future research.

title: Urban disaster risk scenario simulation using an interrelation network of elements at risk: taking flood risk as a case study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University

detail.title: Urban disaster risk scenario simulation using an interrelation network of elements at risk: taking flood risk as a case study
detail.abstract: The combined influence of natural conditions and the dense spatial distribution of elements at risk (EaRs) during rapid urbanization further intensifies the potential for cascading flood impacts. Comprehensive assessment of urban disaster risk and dynamic simulation of risk evolution are therefore essential for enhancing urban natural disaster risk governance capacity. In this study, an improved Implicative Interdependency Model (IIM) is employed to construct an interlayer and intralayer multilevel interrelation network to systematically characterize the geographical and functional interrelations among EaRs. From the perspective of EaRs, a disaster-scenario simulation model is then developed grounded in disaster propagation dynamics, and flood risk in the main urban districts of Changzhou is simulated under varying initial hazard intensity settings. The results demonstrate that incorporating functional interrelations increases the network efficiency of the EaRs interrelation network to 0.1760, exhibiting enhanced connectivity and transmission performance, and strengthening the potential for risk propagation. In addition, flood risk in the study area exhibits a distinct pattern characterized by lower risk in central districts and higher risk in peripheral areas. The disaster evolution process follows a pattern of short-term recovery in the early stage, deterioration in the middle stage, and stabilization in the final stage. Significant differences are also observed among functional zones in terms of response patterns, state evolution trajectories, and resilience thresholds. In particular, the agricultural zone and ecological zone experience relatively severe damage. This study provides decision support and technical reference for identifying high-risk urban flood areas and formulating risk governance strategies.

title: From Behavioral Drives to Motivational Causation Integrating Behavioral and Needs-Based Models in Organizational Assessment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Behavioral Drives to Motivational Causation Integrating Behavioral and Needs-Based Models in Organizational Assessment
detail.abstract: Every day, thousands of organizations use behavioral assessments to hire, develop, and manage their people. Tools like the Predictive Index (among the most widely adopted in the field) promise to reveal what drives employees and how to motivate them. Yet a close look at what these tools actually measure reveals a consequential gap: they describe how people tend to behave, but not why. This paper examines that gap directly.Drawing on foundational motivation theory, peer-reviewed validation research, and applied workforce data, we distinguish between two levels of analysis that are routinely conflated in organizational practice: behavioral description (what people do) and motivational causation (what drives them to do it). We show that widely used behavioral assessments, including the Predictive Index, consistently use the language of "drives," "needs," and "motivation" while measuring constructs operationalized at the level of observable behavior. This creates a systematic interpretive risk we term motivational misattribution: the tendency to treat adaptive responses to unmet needs as stable personality traits.We introduce the AgileBrain framework as a validated, needs-based complement to behavioral assessment. Built on twelve emotional needs organized across four life domains (Self, Material, Social, and Spiritual) AgileBrain directly measures the motivational conditions that generate behavior rather than inferring motivation from behavior itself. Peer-reviewed validation studies demonstrate incremental predictive validity over traditional personality and survey measures. Applied research in the biotechnology sector illustrates how needs-based assessment surfaces the root causes of burnout and attrition that conventional tools routinely miss.We propose a three-layer integrated model of emotional needs → motivational states → behavioral expression that preserves the practical utility of existing behavioral assessments while grounding them in an explicit causal account of human motivation. For practitioners, this reframing has direct implications for how organizations hire, lead, diagnose culture, and design interventions. The goal is not to replace the tools organizations already use, but to explain why those tools work when they do and what to do when they don't.

title: Ecosystemic Internationalization: A Multilevel Framework for Deep-Tech Ventures in Emerging Economies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Ecosystemic Internationalization: A Multilevel Framework for Deep-Tech Ventures in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: Deep-tech ventures face distinctive internationalization challenges shaped by long development cycles, high capital intensity, and dependence on scientific, regulatory, and institutional infrastructures. While innovation ecosystems are increasingly recognized as central to entrepreneurial outcomes, limited research explains how multi-level ecosystem dynamics drive the global expansion of science-based startups in emerging economies. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative investigation grounded in evidence from Brazil, a context combining strong scientific capacity with persistent coordination failures and institutional fragmentation. We propose the Ecosystemic Internationalization Model (EIM), a multilevel framework that reconceptualizes deep-tech internationalization as a distributed, ecosystem-enabled process rather than a firm-level capability. The EIM integrates micro-level actors (entrepreneurs, incubators), meso-level structures (universities, funding agencies, corporate interfaces), macro-level institutions (policies, regulations, international cooperation agreements), and platform infrastructures (digital and organizational intermediaries). Our findings reveal that internationalization trajectories depend critically on alignment and coordination across these layers. Asymmetric ecosystem development, particularly weak digital intermediation and fragmented institutional routines, produces reactive and episodic international engagement, whereas greater ecosystem convergence enables scalable and cumulative global expansion. This study makes three contributions. Theoretically, it extends debates on innovation ecosystems, emerging-economy entrepreneurship, and global innovation networks by foregrounding ecosystem complementarities as drivers of internationalization. Empirically, it provides fine-grained evidence from an underrepresented Latin American context. Practically, the EIM offers a diagnostic tool for policymakers, universities, and incubators seeking to build robust internationalization pathways for science-based ventures in the Global South.

title: From Data to Action: Accelerating Refinery Optimization with AI
affiliations: Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, MOL Group, MOL Group, MOL Group, Budapest University of Technology and Economics and Budapest University of Technology and Economics

detail.title: From Data to Action: Accelerating Refinery Optimization with AI
detail.abstract: Nowadays refinery optimization utilizes sheer amounts of data, which can be handled with modern Linear Programming (LP) software, but the interpreting and applying the results remains challenging. Large petrochemical companies use massive models, with hundreds of thousands of input matrix elements. The LP solution is mathematically correct, but simplifications are made in the model, and data supply errors may occur. Therefore, further insight is needed to trust the results. The LP solver does not have a memory, so additional understanding could be gained by analyzing historical data and comparing it to the current plan. As such, machine learning approaches were suggested to support decision making based on the LP solution. Among these, Anomaly Detection tools are proposed to be used in tandem with the LP output. A transformed version of the popular ECOD methodology is applied. New methods are proposed to handle high-dimensional data: choosing the most informative pairs. Then, this is used alongside two 2D Anomaly Detection algorithms, revealing several business opportunities and data supply errors in the MOL refinery scheduling and planning architecture.

title: The Impact of Business Internship–Developed Skills on Graduate Employability
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Dartmouth and Department of Communication Disorders Sciences

detail.title: The Impact of Business Internship–Developed Skills on Graduate Employability
detail.abstract: Most research on the link between internship-developed soft skills and graduate employability remains largely theoretical and prescriptive, with limited empirical validation. To address this gap, this study developed and tested a model—grounded in human capital, social cognitive, social exchange, and signaling theories—that explains how employability skills (ES) shape graduate employability (GE). Using data from business interns at a comprehensive Arabian university, the model identifies social intelligence (SI), self-reliance (SR), and work ethic (WE) as key predictors of GE, with SI exerting the strongest direct and indirect effects. These higher-order skills enhance employability as employers increasingly value graduates who pair technical competence with initiative, persistence, and strong collaborative abilities. Despite certain limitations, the findings clarify the role of internship-developed skills in preparing graduates for the workforce and support more effective planning and evaluation of work-integrated learning (WIL) programs.

title: Apparent hydraulic memory in pressurized slug tests: A lagging-theory analytical solution and uncertainty diagnostics
affiliations: Chung Yuan Christian University and Chung Yuan Christian University

detail.title: Apparent hydraulic memory in pressurized slug tests: A lagging-theory analytical solution and uncertainty diagnostics
detail.abstract: Delayed recovery in pressurized slug tests can carry information about near-well hydraulic memory, but the same short records also reflect wellbore storage, pressure amplitude, support scale, and model non-uniqueness. This study develops an observation-to-memory transformation framework that extracts apparent-memory diagnostics from pressurized slug tests with explicit uncertainty checks. A new radial analytical solution embeds Lagging Theory within the classical state-factor form and introduces separate response times for flux memory and hydraulic-gradient memory. The solution reduces to the classical instantaneous-flow response when lag effects vanish. We evaluated the framework with tabulated Minnelusa aquifer slug-test records from three wells near Spearfish, South Dakota. The analysis combined classical and lagging-theory pathways, deterministic fitting, Bayesian posterior sampling, response-level residual diagnostics, load-block validation, posterior principal-component analysis, and a hierarchical pressure-dependent model for repeated tests in one well. The lagging-theory pathway reduced structured residuals, but the inferred delay times did not behave as universally identifiable aquifer constants. Repeated partial-release tests at one well supported a comparatively stable shared-memory interpretation, whereas repeated pressure-amplitude tests at another well produced pressure-dependent apparent memory. In the multi-pressure well, the median flux-memory response time increased from 2.50 s at 5 psi to 61.7 s at 30 psi, and the apparent memory length increased almost linearly with pressure amplitude. Load-block validation improved average withheld-pressure prediction, but three pressure levels were insufficient to define a general pressure-lag law. Pressurized slug tests can therefore screen for delayed hydraulic response and classify memory behavior; unique material interpretation still requires independent constraints on wellbore response, support scale, and pressure-dependent near-well effects.

title: Adaptive Stacked Ensemble Fusion: Bayesian Porosity Inference in Alluvial Aquifers When the Errors Are Not Independent
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Tirana and Polytechnic University of Tirana

detail.title: Adaptive Stacked Ensemble Fusion: Bayesian Porosity Inference in Alluvial Aquifers When the Errors Are Not Independent
detail.abstract: When hydrogeologists estimate effective porosity from two indirect methods — grain-size correlations and hydraulic inversions — they almost always combine the estimates by inverse-variance weighting, the textbook formula. That formula assumes the two errors are independent. They are not. In alluvial aquifers, both methods see the world through the same grain-size lens, and when the lens is foggy in fine-grained facies, both estimates drift together. The result is a posterior that looks confident and is wrong. Here we develop Adaptive Stacked Ensemble Fusion (ASEF), a framework that takes the error correlation seriously: it models the correlation as a facies-dependent random variable, derives the combination weights from leave-one-out cross-validation rather than from assumed variances, and updates everything iteratively against nitrate observations. We then prove a phase-boundary theorem: the fusion problem partitions sharply along the line σKC/σVS=1/|ρ| . Below it, the value of ASEF is that uncertainty becomes honest; above it, the variance itself drops by 30–70%. Practitioners can read off the regime before running anything. We test the framework on 43 wells across the 1,200 km² Tirana–Fushë-Kuqe–Lezhë alluvial aquifer in Albania, with priors transferred openly from two well-characterized analog systems (Cape Cod glacial outwash, Borden braided-stream alluvium) because direct laboratory porosity at regional scale is not feasible — a limitation we name rather than hide. A wholly independent USGS lithostratigraphic boring at Cape Cod, Massachusetts (26 grain-size samples, 11 hydrostratigraphic units) sits squarely in the above-boundary regime and verifies the prediction: variance reductions of 30–70% occur exactly where the theory says they should. The classical assumption of independent pathway errors has produced over-confident porosity inferences in alluvial aquifer studies for decades. ASEF gives that confidence back its honesty, at almost no additional computational cost, and tells anyone willing to plot two numbers whether the correction will matter in their site.

title: Fuzzy-Gated Verification of LLM Agents for Industrial Fault Diagnosis: An Evolutionary-Optimized Closed-Loop Framework
affiliations: Peking University, Peking University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nantong University and Peking University

detail.title: Fuzzy-Gated Verification of LLM Agents for Industrial Fault Diagnosis: An Evolutionary-Optimized Closed-Loop Framework
detail.abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis and machine health management are essential for reliable operation of industrial systems, yet deploying large language models (LLMs) for these tasks introduces reliability risks including hallucinated evidence, overconfident outputs, and inconsistent reasoning. We propose CL-LLMOps, a closed-loop LLMOps framework that orchestrates LLM agents through five integrated stages—from alarm normalization to regression-tested action. At the semantic verification level—where, to our knowledge, soft computing has not previously been applied—its hierarchical mechanism combines rule-based pattern checking, cross-attention evidence scoring, and Mamdani fuzzy inference gating, jointly optimized via multi-objective particle swarm optimization, to detect hallucinations and evidence contradictions before maintenance decisions. Evaluation on three public datasets spanning power quality classification, bearing fault diagnosis, and wind turbine SCADA anomaly detection—validated across two open-source LLM backbones (Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B)—shows that CL-LLMOps achieves 98.6% diagnostic accuracy on power quality data, 99.3% on CWRU bearing data, and 95.2% on CARE wind turbine data. The framework reduces inconsistency-type hallucination from 12% to 2% relative to the fine-tuned LLM baseline while maintaining 93% action accuracy and 96% risk compliance on PQ data, with fuzzy gating specifically improving action accuracy by 5 percentage points through graded borderline handling. This work bridges LLM-powered intelligence and operational dependability for industrial deployment, offering a novel integration of established soft computing techniques—neural attention, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary optimization—at the semantic verification level for deploying trustworthy AI agents in fault diagnosis under the Industry 5.0 paradigm.

title: Beyond Perceived Usefulness: The Dominant Role of Shariah Compliance and Religious Obligation in Islamic Mobile Financial Services Adoption
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond Perceived Usefulness: The Dominant Role of Shariah Compliance and Religious Obligation in Islamic Mobile Financial Services Adoption
detail.abstract: Islamic Mobile Financial Services (Islamic MFS) represent a rapidly growing yet theoretically underdeveloped segment of global financial services. This study examines the determinants of adoption and actual use behavior among Shariah-minded users by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with two faith-based constructs: Islamic Shariah Compliance (ISC) and Religious Obligation (RO). Using PLS-SEM on a sample of 312 Islamic MFS users in Bangladesh, the study finds that ISC is the dominant predictor of attitude (β = 0.699), while Perceived Usefulness is non-significant — directly inverting the standard TAM prediction. Subjective Norm is the strongest predictor of behavioral intention (β = 0.467), and Religious Obligation uniquely drives actual use behavior directly (β = 0.307), bypassing the standard intention-behavior pathway. These findings establish that faith-compliance signaling — not functional utility — is the primary marketing lever for Islamic MFS providers, with significant implications for segmentation, positioning, and communication strategy in Islamic financial services markets.

title: What Should Be Automated in Offices? Occupants’ Preferences for Automation Levels from a Large Survey in Spain and the Netherlands
affiliations: , Delft University of Technology, Delft University of Technology and Delft University of Technology

detail.title: What Should Be Automated in Offices? Occupants’ Preferences for Automation Levels from a Large Survey in Spain and the Netherlands
detail.abstract: Occupant-centered building control requires defining not only which building services should be automated but also the role occupants prefer to retain in the control loop. However, empirical evidence remains fragmented across single services, leaving a gap in understanding how preferred automation levels varies across building services and daily routines. This study establishes an evidence-based typology for occupant-centered building automation, mapping preferences across ten services and three workday phases through a large-scale questionnaire of 3,504 office workers in the Netherlands and Spain. Using a consistent five-level automation scale, we map preferences across ten building services and three distinct workday phases (arrival, active work, and leaving). Results show that automation preferences are context-dependent, varying according to the specific building service and the current workday phase. HVAC systems, particularly mechanical ventilation, show the strongest acceptance of automated control, whereas directly reachable elements, such as openable windows and personal devices, are predominantly preferred under manual control. A primary finding of this study is the prevalence of 'mixed-control' profiles (61.5% of respondents), showing that occupants' desire for personal control is service-dependent. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence of the interaction strategy gap, demonstrating that higher automation acceptance is statistically contingent upon digital, desk-reachable, and information-rich control interfaces. Prior experience with automated systems emerged as the most consistent predictor of acceptance of automation, suggesting that trust in the control loop is experience-based. These findings argue against one-size-fits-all automation and provide empirical basis for designing adaptive, service-specific control strategies that balance building energy goals with occupant agency.

title: Trends and determinants of dairy co-operative performance in Zambia: a mixed-methods analysis in Namwala District ​
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Zambia, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Belgrade, Kapasa Makasa University, Mukuba University and University of Belgrade

detail.title: Trends and determinants of dairy co-operative performance in Zambia: a mixed-methods analysis in Namwala District ​
detail.abstract: This study examines the performance of six dairy co-operatives in Namwala District, Zambia, over a decade (2014–2023) using a convergent mixed-methods design. Quantitative analysis employed descriptive statistics and OLS regression on a balanced panel of 40 co-operative-year observations, while qualitative insights were derived from five focus group discussions with 75 participants (25 female, 50 male). Membership grew from 412 to 2,000 (CAGR 19.2%), yet milk production exhibited marked volatility, ranging from 389,000 to 1,910,000 litres annually. Regression analysis reveals a significant negative relationship between membership and per-farmer productivity (β = −3.48, p < 0.001), indicating a dilution effect whereby membership expansion outpaces productive capacity. Milk price positively predicted total production (β = 14.48, p = 0.035), while the revenue model (adjusted R² = 0.941) confirms that production volume and price, not membership size, drive co-operative income. Focus group discussions identified drought, feed scarcity, governance instability, and inadequate veterinary services as principal constraints, while also documenting the emergence of informal milk trading networks as adaptive institutional responses. The study concludes that membership-driven scaling without parallel investment in productive capacity undermines individual farmer returns, and recommends productivity-first growth strategies, governance strengthening, climate-resilient infrastructure, and quality-based pricing to sustain co-operative performance.

title: How does monetary policy affect corporate innovation along the supply chain? The role of suppliers' financial multiplier
affiliations: Peking University, Guanghua School of Management, Students, Nankai University, Nankai University and Nankai University

detail.title: How does monetary policy affect corporate innovation along the supply chain? The role of suppliers' financial multiplier
detail.abstract: This study presents granular evidence that highly leveraged suppliers magnify the propagation of contractionary monetary policy shocks through supply chains. Drawing on Chinese supply-chain data covering 2015Q1–2024Q1, we find that monetary tightening triggers sharper declines in innovation among downstream customers tied to high-leverage suppliers than among those linked to low-leverage suppliers. Mechanism analysis reveals that, when suppliers are highly leveraged, tightening monetary conditions disrupt supplier–customer relationships and dampen knowledge diffusion along the supply chain, thereby eroding downstream innovation. Moreover, this amplification is especially pronounced when suppliers provide more relationship-specific inputs and when customers face higher switching costs.

title: BRICS AI Governance: Comparative Analysis of Public-Policy Approaches of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and Indonesia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BRICS AI Governance: Comparative Analysis of Public-Policy Approaches of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and Indonesia
detail.abstract: The 2025 BRICS Leaders’ Statement advocates for multilateral Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance, interoperable standards, and greater Global South integration in digital policy. Premised on the view that leveraging existing cooperative frameworks is more pragmatic than establishing new international organizations, this paper addresses a critical gap by analyzing AI policy convergences and divergences within the BRICS+ bloc. Employing qualitative methods, including thematic and discourse analysis, we evaluate the AI strategies, laws, and regulatory frameworks of the bloc's five largest economies: China, India, Russia, Indonesia, and Brazil. Our comparative analysis reveals distinct national regulatory profiles. China leads in binding, application-specific AI regulations, while Brazil adopts an EU-inspired, rights-based approach. India pursues a pro-innovation model anchored in robust digital public infrastructure (DPI), Russia prioritizes technological sovereignty driven by geopolitical realities, and Indonesia explores a diverse, flexible regulatory mix. Despite these varied trajectories, we identify significant areas of policy convergence. To foster a unified and proactive BRICS stance on AI and digital communications policy, we recommend targeted collaborative pathways. These include joint research on risk-assessment and safety standards, shared computing infrastructure, cross-border regulatory sandboxes, and the collaborative development of local-language models.

title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment
detail.abstract: As the global energy transition matures, analytical focus has shifted from isolated engineering performance toward integrated system-level economic efficiency. While the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) remains the universal metric for evaluating project viability, traditional models are largely static, failing to incorporate the profound financial impacts of supply chain performance, logistical volatility, and institutional constraints. This study addresses these "integration gaps" by examining the relationship between logistical system conditions, operational disruptions, and sustainability outcomes.Adopting a critical realist perspective and a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the research utilizes semi-structured interviews with industry experts to identify sources of operational friction, followed by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and the development of an Integrated LCOE (I-LCOE) model. Central to the study is the Dynamic Logistics–Sustainability Integration Model, which conceptualizes renewable energy systems as interconnected layers where logistical agility directly influences financial risk.The findings establish logistics as a primary structural cost driver embedded across all project lifecycle phases. The research identifies "logistical velocity" as a critical determinant of the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), as supply chain friction serves as an aggressive risk multiplier that inflates investor risk premiums. Furthermore, physical upscaling of components introduces non-linear logistical constraints that traditional models fail to capture. The study proposes an integrated digital knowledge management platform to resolve information asymmetry. By internalizing traditionally externalized variables such as geopolitical disruptions at maritime chokepoints this research provides a transformative framework for achieving SDG 7 and optimizing the systemic costs of global decarbonization.

title: A NEW AGE QUANTUM VEDIC LEADERSHIP MODEL: INTEGRATING ANCIENT WISDOM WITH NON-LINEAR ECONOMETRICS
affiliations: SMART international Holdings, Inc. and Bank Dhofar SAOG

detail.title: A NEW AGE QUANTUM VEDIC LEADERSHIP MODEL: INTEGRATING ANCIENT WISDOM WITH NON-LINEAR ECONOMETRICS
detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel, multi-disciplinary management paradigm that bridges ancient Vedic philosophy through the mathematical and cosmic properties of number 9 (Nava) and Vortex Mathematics with contemporary quantum leadership in a non-linear econometric framework. It re-conceptualizes that a firm is not as a static container, but an entangled, algorithmically orchestrated node within a co-emergent market field. It develops a non-linear differential model using constrained transcendental regression to isolate the "Invariant Vision Constant" scalar, alongside a first-order autoregressive difference equation to map Golden Ratio-governed corporate feedback loops. The model is empirically validated using a longitudinal, six-year dataset (including one-year forecasts) across top eleven US corporations, evaluating the interplay between Strategy, Structure, Culture, Operations and operational friction. The empirical analysis confirms that massive infrastructure scaling introduces temporary, unmanifested structural drag before hitting operational resonance. Long-term strategic success relies on a leader's ability to act as a coherent signal within environmental noise, shifting internal organizational frequencies to collapse boundaries between corporate agency and market structure. This non-linear model demonstrates a superior capacity to map path-dependent choices and structural efficiencies compared to conventional linear management frameworks.

title: From Tool to Platform: Road Pricing and the Theory of Public Governance Real Options
affiliations: University of Melbourne

detail.title: From Tool to Platform: Road Pricing and the Theory of Public Governance Real Options
detail.abstract: Real options theory has proven a powerful lens for understanding strategic investment decisions under uncertainty, yet its application to public governance contexts has remained largely metaphorical, importing financial assumptions without interrogating their domain specificity. This paper proposes a systematic mapping between real options theory and urban road pricing, revealing that road pricing — understood as an institutional platform rather than a congestion management tool — instantiates and extends real options logic in ways that generate a theoretically significant departure from financial option theory. Through systematic analysis of ten real options components (underlying asset, option premium, strike price, volatility, time to expiration, exercise decision, option types, option holder, irreversibility, and compound structure), we identify ten corresponding systematic departures from standard financial assumptions: constitutive asset endogeneity, recoverable premiums, manipulable strike prices, multidimensional volatility portfolios, ambiguous expiration windows, graduated exercise, simultaneous multi-type option generation, recursive compound structure, distributed option holding, and generative irreversibility. Together, these departures constitute the foundations of a theory of public governance real options as a distinct analytical category. Illustrative cases from Singapore, Stockholm, and New York elaborate the theoretical framework, demonstrating its capacity to explain implementation outcomes that existing theory cannot adequately address. The framework resolves a central paradox in road pricing scholarship — that road pricing is simultaneously a cause and consequence of successful urban governance — by revealing the recursive, constitutive logic of governance platforms operating under radical uncertainty. We propose public governance real options as a theoretical category that reframes governance investment decisions — from road pricing to digital infrastructure and environmental policy — as platform-building exercises whose strategic value lies not in what they deliver but in the option space they create.

title: The Impact of Bank Technology Loans on Corporate R&D Spending: Evidence from China
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics and William Paterson University - Cotsakos College of Business

detail.title: The Impact of Bank Technology Loans on Corporate R&D Spending: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: Bank technology loans are of great significance for improving enterprise innovation quality and cultivating new-quality productive forces. Using a sample of 37 industrial sectors in China from 2008 to 2022, this paper classifies industries into hard-tech and non-hard-tech categories to examine the impact of technology loans on innovation quality and its underlying mechanisms. The findings show that technology loans have a positive effect on innovation quality in both categories, with a stronger effect in hard-tech industries. The promoting effect of technology loans on disruptive innovation exhibits a significant lag, indicating that disruptive innovation requires the sustained support of "patient capital." In terms of transmission mechanisms, self-funded R&D investment plays a full mediating role in hard-tech industries, while no mediating effect is found in non-hard-tech industries. Regarding R&D structure, technology loans significantly increase investment in the technology development stage in hard-tech industries, fully mediating innovation quality through this channel, but have no significant effect on technology acquisition investment.
